chapter: Harlem musicians and the road with Armstrong
title: Bill Coleman in the band and listening to 'Feelin' the Spirit' and 'Josie Lightning'
summary: Holmes identifies the soloists on two flag-wavers, including himself, and explains that the written parts had been played many times before recording.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: Now, Russell made some recordings with Bill Coleman in the band. Was he ever regular in the band?
Bill, he was in there regularly.
So he wasn't just added for the recordings.
No. He was in the band later. But he stayed on. I don't know how long he stayed. Well, I don't know what recordings he ever made. But he made some. But he wasn't in a lot of them.
[PAUSE]
"Feeling The Spirit" and we'll spot the... [PLAYS "FEELIN' THE SPIRIT"] Higgy.
Higgenbotham. Albert Nicholas, clarinet. [TROMBONE SOLO] J.C. Higgenbotham, trombone... [TRUMPET SOLO] Bill Coleman, trumpet... [ENSEMBLE]
Are you reading?
Oh yeah. Yeah, we're reading. Some of us are reading. [SINGER] J.C. Higgenbotham, scat-singing. [TENOR SOLO] Teddy Hill... [CLARINET OVER ENSEMBLE] Red Allen.
[MUSIC ENDS]
I'd like to do the same for "Josie Lightning," which was another flag-waver.
[PLAYS "JOSIE LIGHTNING"]
[CLARINET OPENING SOLO] [THEN PIANO] That was Russell.
Oh, Luis Russell, piano. [AFTER BASS SOLO
AGAINST ENSEMBLE, THERE'S A TRUMPET SOLO] Red Allen. [FAST ENNSEMBLE]
Reading again?
Yeah. [TROMBONE SOLO] J.C. Higgenbotham. [ALTO SOLO 8 BARS]
Charlie Holmes.
[TROMBONE, 8 BARS, THEN TRUMPET SOLO] That's Red. [CLARINET SOLO] Albert Nicholas. ["JOSIE LIGHTNING" ENDS]
On those parts where you're reading, that wouldn't have been the first time you were seeing that music, was it?
No, that had been played many a time before we recorded it.
But you brought the music in with you and had it...

Oh yeah. They carried the music like you carry in your saxophone. Because they had a whole thing full of books, and everybody... Each book was about that thick with music. They had plenty of music to read. And it was tough reading, too, in them days -- tough arrangements.
